parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what actually moves in a wave - the particles wobble about a fixed point while something else travels forward. What are those two directions for sound?
parts.proper_answer: The oscillations of the particles are parallel to the direction of transfer of energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Particles and Energy**
Imagine a sound wave travelling forward. The air particles do not travel with it, they just vibrate back and forth about their equilibrium positions. In a longitudinal wave that back-and-forth line is along the same line as the wave is travelling.

Step 2: **State the Definition**
So you can say it simply as: $$ \text{particle oscillation direction is parallel to energy direction} $$ That contrast with a transverse wave where they are perpendicular.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: relative motion of source and observer
hints: Hint 1: The horn always emits 1.2 kHz, but the vehicle is going round in a circle while the observer stays still. When during the circle is the vehicle getting closer to the observer and when is it getting further away?
Hint 2: Recall how motion towards you crowds wavefronts together and motion away stretches them apart. How does that change the wavelength and frequency you detect?
parts.proper_answer: The vehicle moves relative to the stationary observer. When the component of its velocity is towards the observer the observed frequency is higher than 1.2 kHz, and when the component is away from the observer the observed frequency is lower than 1.2 kHz.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Relative Motion Around the Circle**
The source frequency stays at $1.2\text{ kHz}$. What changes is the radial motion - the part of the velocity along the line to the distant observer. For half the lap the vehicle has a component towards the observer, for the other half it has a component away.

Step 2: **Link Motion to Observed Frequency**
Moving towards crowds the wavefronts ahead of the source, so the observed wavelength $\lambda_o$ is shorter and $$ f_o = \frac{v}{\lambda_o} $$ is higher than $1.2\text{ kHz}$. Moving away stretches the wavefronts, so $\lambda_o$ is longer and $f_o$ is lower than $1.2\text{ kHz}$. That is why Fig. 4.2 oscillates above and below $1.2\text{ kHz}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: What is the standard name for the change in observed frequency when a wave source moves relative to an observer?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Name the Effect**
A change in observed frequency due to relative motion of source and observer is called the Doppler effect. Here it applies to sound waves from the moving horn.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.2 at time T - is the detected frequency at a maximum, a minimum or in the middle? What source motion gives that extreme?
parts.proper_answer: X at the top (12 o'clock) position of the track, where velocity is directly towards the observer giving maximum frequency.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the Graph at Time T**
In Fig. 4.2 at time $T$ the frequency is $1.40\text{ kHz}$, a maximum. A maximum means the source is moving directly towards the distant observer with the largest approach speed.

Step 2: **Find That Point on the Circle**
The observer is far to the east. Directly eastward motion happens at the northmost point of the clockwise track. At the west side shown the vehicle moves roughly north, at the top it moves due east. So mark X at the top of the circle.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Time 9T/4 is 2T + T/4, a quarter of a period after a maximum in Fig. 4.2. What is the frequency doing there, and what does that tell you about motion towards or away from the observer?
parts.proper_answer: Y at the right-hand edge (3 o'clock) position of the track, closest to the observer, where motion is transverse to the line to the observer.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Locate 9T/4 on the Graph**
$$ \frac{9T}{4} = 2T + \frac{T}{4} $$ At $2T$ there is a maximum $1.40\text{ kHz}$. A quarter period later the curve is falling through $1.2\text{ kHz}$. That is the zero-shift point where radial velocity is zero.

Step 2: **Translate to the Track**
Starting from the top (max towards) and moving one quarter lap clockwise brings the vehicle to the eastmost point, nearest the observer. There its velocity is due south, perpendicular to the line to the observer, so no Doppler shift. Mark Y at the right-hand edge (3 o'clock).

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Read the extreme frequency off Fig. 4.2 - what is the highest value of f reached when the vehicle comes straight towards the observer?
Hint 2: Think about which version of the Doppler formula applies for approach: does the denominator become v - vs or v + vs, and what are fs, v and fo?
Hint 3: You now have one equation with one unknown vs. How can you rearrange to solve for the vehicle speed before putting numbers in?
parts.proper_answer: Maximum $f_o = 1.40\text{ kHz} = 1.40 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$. For approach, $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$, so $1.40 \times 10^3 = (1.2 \times 10^3 \times 320)/(320 - v_s)$ giving $v_s = 46\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the Maximum Frequency from the Graph**
The largest Doppler shift is easiest to use. From Fig. 4.2 the peaks are at: $$ f_{max} = 1.40\text{ kHz} = 1.40 \times 10^3\text{ Hz} $$ The emitted frequency is $$ f_s = 1.2\text{ kHz} $$ and speed of sound $$ v = 320\text{ m s}^{-1} $$

Step 2: **Apply the Doppler Equation for Approach**
For a source moving towards a stationary observer: $$ f_o = f_s \frac{v}{v - v_s} $$ Put in the maximum values: $$ 1.40 \times 10^3 = 1.2 \times 10^3 \times \frac{320}{320 - v_s} $$ You could equally use the minimum $1.05\text{ kHz}$ with $v + v_s$ in the denominator.

Step 3: **Solve for the Vehicle Speed**
Rearrange: $$ 320 - v_s = \frac{1.2 \times 320}{1.40} $$ $$ 320 - v_s \approx 274 $$ $$ v_s \approx 320 - 274 = 46\text{ m s}^{-1} $$ That is fast but reasonable for a vehicle, and it is much less than the speed of sound as expected.
